entry.title: Environmental Impacts of Aquaculture and Risks of Antibiotic Use

link.title: Environmental Impacts of Aquaculture and Risks of Antibiotic Use

entry.content:
Aquaculture is the controlled farming of aquatic species in freshwater, brackish-water, and marine environments. It includes breeding, rearing (growing juvenile animals to full size), and harvesting. Aquaculture has emerged as a way to sustain population growth, meet global seafood demand, and reduce dependence on wild-caught species, but it can also present a wide range of environmental, ecological, and biological challenges depending on the farming practices and species involved.

Aquaculture as an Alternative to Wild-Caught Fisheries

Since ancient times, humans have depended heavily on fisheries as an important source of food. Over the last few decades, as the human population has grown rapidly, demand for aquatic food has also grown, leading to increasing pressure on natural supplies. Fish stocks eventually became severely strained from the 1980s through the early 2000s [1]. Driven by increasing fish shortages, food security needs, the drive for exports, and rising living standards, commercial aquaculture developed into a highly viable and organised industry. Since the early 1980s, aquaculture production has expanded exponentially, making it one of the fastest-growing sectors of global food production, especially in developing nations [2,3]. However, aquaculture comes with its own caveats.

Classic concerns around aquaculture

🪵 Habitat Loss and Habitat Destruction

Establishing aquatic farming zones can require the conversion of natural habitats into farmable areas, directly or indirectly causing the degradation or destruction of local ecosystems. This concern is particularly associated with the loss of mangrove forests and other coastal ecosystems to shrimp farms and other forms of brackish-water farming, such as milkfish, tilapia, and mud crabs [4].

ℹ Mangrove loss has been a major concern amid aquaculture expansion and climate change. A large proportion of mangrove loss was caused by human activities, which were mainly concentrated in Southeast Asia, with Indonesia, Myanmar, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam accounting for nearly 80% of global direct human-driven loss. Mangrove conversion for aquaculture and agriculture, particularly rice, shrimp, and oil palm farming, was the primary driver of anthropogenic loss [5]. However, in the past decade, mangrove loss rates have slowed significantly, with natural and climate-related losses becoming increasingly prominent, while human-driven losses have shown a decline. Meanwhile, mangrove gains have increased. These shifts might be the result of several factors, including natural seaward expansion (the main driver), conservation efforts, and a lack of remaining mangrove forests available for conversion [5,6].

☣️ Water pollution & Disease Outbreaks

Aquaculture can involve intensive treatment of water and surrounding areas with chemicals and pesticides, as well as the use of antibiotics and other veterinary medications. These substances, together with waste products, can enter the natural environment and affect aquatic life, causing problems such as harmful algal blooms†, dead zones‡, and diseases that could lead to massive die-offs [4]. Additionally, aquaculture often involves high stocking densities that can increase the risk of disease outbreaks, which may spread to wild populations and threaten natural ecosystems [7].

🦠 Antibiotics resistance & exposure

Antibiotics are the most used veterinary drugs in aquaculture for disease management and growth promotion, but their use presents substantial risks to wildlife and human health. Improper use of antibiotics can promote antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (“superbugs”) that are not only difficult to treat, but can also carry antibiotic resistance genes that may be transferred to other bacteria, potentially affecting animals and humans. Residual antibiotics in the tissues of farmed aquatic animals can also pose direct health risks to humans, including severe allergic reactions, disruption of the gut microbiota, systemic organ toxicity, and potential carcinogenic effects [8,9].

⚠️ The most concerning aquaculture products regarding veterinary drug residues

𓆛 Chinese Tilapia

Chinese Tilapia in a supermarket. Photo by Terrance Barksdale (Pexels).

China is the world’s largest seafood producer and the country that consumes the most antibiotics in aquaculture, accounting for 57.9% of global antimicrobial consumption in 2017. It has also been the world’s largest exporter of tilapia in international markets for decades, and tilapia is one of the species raised with the highest use of antibiotics [10]. China is among the countries with the highest rates of inspection violations involving antibiotic use in aquaculture products imported into the US. In EU markets, Chinese tilapia is the second most frequently flagged product for veterinary drug residues [11,12].

𓆞 Vietnamese Catfish/Pangasius (“Basa”)

Pangasius/Basa fish - AI-generated image.

Vietnam is the world’s largest exporter of catfish, most commonly pangasius species, and the fourth-largest consumer of antibiotics in aquaculture after China, India, and Indonesia, accounting for 5% of global consumption [10]. Vietnam also has the highest number of violations alongside China related to illegal veterinary drug use in farmed fish exported to the US and has notoriously been a top offender for similar violations in other imported aquaculture products across other major markets. Its catfish is among the most rejected shipments globally due to antibiotic violations [11,12].

Vietnamese, Indian, Indonesian, and Chinese Shrimp/Prawn

Whiteleg shrimp (also known as Pacific white shrimp; scientific name: Litopenaeus vannamei), the most commonly farmed and imported shrimp species. Photo by Viet Chi Go (Pexels).

Shrimp and prawn are the most exported aquaculture products worldwide by volume. Historically, Ecuador, India, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Argentina were the five leading exporters, respectively [13]. However, the ranking has shifted since 2024, with Indonesia overtaking Vietnam as the third-largest exporter, Argentina moving into fourth place, and Thailand taking fifth [14]. China is the world’s largest producer of shrimp and prawn but exports far less than other major producers because of its huge domestic demand. Nevertheless, it remains a top exporter of processed and value-added shrimp products, mainly to Japan, South Korea, and Southeast Asia [15].

Among these leading exporters, shrimp and prawn products from Vietnam, India, Indonesia, and China are the most frequently rejected in major markets for containing banned veterinary drugs, followed by Bangladesh, a significant exporter to EU markets, and Malaysia, a prominent re-exporter of Chinese products [12].

𓎿 Chilean Salmon

Salmon fillet. Photo by Deane Bayas (Pexels).

Chile is the world's second-largest producer of farmed salmon after Norway, but its salmon industry has been associated with exceptionally high antibiotic use. Between 2011 and 2015, Chilean salmon farms used more than 1,500 times as much antibiotics per tonne of salmon as Norwegian farms, and may have used much more than any other salmon producer. This intensive use has raised concerns about antibiotic-resistant bacteria, with superbugs having been detected around salmon farms in Chile [4,16].

The biggest import markets for Chilean salmon are the US, Japan, and Brazil [17]. Amid growing global demand for safer products and increasing concerns about antimicrobial resistance, the Chilean government and industry partners have advanced initiatives and programmes to address antibiotic use in salmon farming. These include CSARP [18], developed in partnership with the Monterey Bay Aquarium and the One Health-based National Action Plan (NAP) [19], led by the University of Chile in collaboration with several government bodies and funded by ICARS*, both of which aim to reduce antimicrobial resistance and antibiotic use in Chilean Atlantic salmon aquaculture.

Risks of consuming aquaculture products with antibiotic residues

Developed nations: low to moderate.

Developing nations: medium to high.

The risk of consumer exposure to veterinary drug residues in imported aquaculture products is low to moderate in developed markets, including high-income European countries, the US, Japan, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia, where strict regulations and zero-tolerance policies for certain unapproved veterinary drugs, including banned antibiotics such as nitrofurans and chloramphenicol, require non-compliant consignments to be destroyed or returned to the country of origin. However, the underlying concern persists because the global aquaculture industry continues to rely heavily on antimicrobials, and products containing illicit or unapproved veterinary drugs are still frequently flagged at border controls. Moreover, imported aquaculture and seafood products are usually tested through risk-based sampling rather than screening every shipment; therefore, non-compliant products may occasionally bypass screening, although the risk is low [20].

Prominent global reference points for drug and veterinary residue standards include Codex Alimentarius§, the European Union, and the United States; a lot of other countries defer to these as baselines for their own regulations. Low- and middle-income countries tend to follow Codex maximum residue limits (MRLs), while the EU, US, and a few other developed nations establish their own standards [21]. However, many countries, especially developing nations, still lack comprehensive national frameworks for regulating veterinary drug residues, or apply standards that are less stringent than Codex recommendations [22].

Overall, the EU, EEA countries, and Switzerland maintain the most stringent regulatory frameworks for veterinary drug residues and use [23]. On the other hand, developing nations and major seafood-exporting countries, such as China, India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Vietnam, have much less robust controls, particularly in their domestic markets. Other developed countries, including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, generally maintain well-established regulatory frameworks but allow more flexibility in drug use and residue limits than the EU.

➡️ Consumers can minimise their risk of exposure by choosing products with clear labelling and transparent sourcing information, or opting for products from countries or producers with stricter controls on antibiotic use and veterinary drug residues, and a better track record of compliance with food safety regulations.

What are the Safest parts of fish and crustaceans to consume

🐟 Lean Fish meat ✓

Antibiotic residues and environmental contaminants tend to accumulate and persist in fish brains, livers, muscles, gonads, fatty tissues, and other organs [24,25]. Therefore, removing the head (including the brain and gills), skin, belly fat, dark meat, and all internal organs, as well as trimming excess fat and the tail, before consumption may help reduce exposure [26]. However, drug residues and contaminants can also be present in lean muscle meat, making seafood from trusted sources the safest choice.

California OEHHA’s recommended guide to fish preparation. Image by OEHHA.

🦐 Crustacean Muscle Meat ✓

In crustaceans such as shrimp, prawns, crabs, lobsters, and crayfish, drug residues and environmental contaminants typically concentrate in the hepatopancreas (the yellowish, creamy, mustard-like substance in their heads), gills, shells, and digestive tracts (the intestine, visible as the dark vein running along the back of shrimp, prawn, lobster, and crayfish tails) [27]. Many regulatory bodies, such as the FDA, recommend consuming only lean meat from the body, claws, and tail to minimise exposure to such toxins. As with fish, choosing seafood from trusted sources remains the most effective way to avoid eating unwanted substances.

Recommended parts of shrimp and crab for safer consumption: body meat, tail meat, and claw meat. AI-generated image.

Choosing Seafood More Responsibly

Consumers can consult international seafood certifications, such as MSC and ASC, or their country's seafood safety and sustainability guidelines. For veterinary drug residues, check the product's country of origin and sourcing transparency, and consult your regional food-safety authority for applicable residue limits and import controls. Prominent resources include:

  • Seafood Watch by the Monterey Bay Aquarium (US): seafoodwatch.org
  • Mr.GoodFish (a programme funded by the EU): mrgoodfish.com
  • GoodFish by the Australian Marine Conservation Society (Australia): goodfish.org.au
  • Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) certification for farmed seafood: asc-aqua.org
  • Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification for wild-caught seafood: msc.org

BAP, ASC, and MSC labels for certified aquaculture and wild-caught seafood products.

†Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs): rapid overgrowth of algae, often driven by excessive nutrient levels and favourable environmental conditions, such as warm temperatures, that can harm people, animals, and aquatic ecosystems.

‡Dead Zones: areas in aquatic environments where dissolved oxygen levels become too low to support most organisms.

*ICARS: International Centre for Antimicrobial Resistance Solutions

§Codex Alimentarius: a collection of international food standards, guidelines, and codes of practice developed by the FAO and WHO to protect consumer health and promote fair practices in food trade.

entry.summary: Explore the environmental impacts of aquaculture, from habitat destruction and water pollution to antibiotic overuse, antimicrobial resistance, and veterinary drug residues in seafood. Learn how farming practices affect ecosystems and food safety, and how to make more informed seafood choices

entry.title: Where Does Glucosamine Come From? Commercial Glucosamine Supplement Sources and Their Impacts

link.title: Where Does Glucosamine Come From? Commercial Glucosamine Supplement Sources and Their Impacts

entry.content:
Where Does Glucosamine Exist in Nature?

Glucosamine is one of the most abundant amino sugars (modified monosaccharides) found in living organisms. In humans, it is an important compound involved in building and maintaining joints and cartilage. However, unlike other bioactive compounds such as certain vitamins or fatty acids, glucosamine is not a nutrient that needs to come directly from food. The human body makes its own glucosamine by converting blood glucose (a simple sugar) and glutamine (an amino acid made by the body or obtained from protein-rich foods) through a series of chemical reactions [1]. The resulting glucosamine is then used to make larger molecules that form important parts of cartilage, connective tissues, and synovial fluid.

Glucosamine is not unique to humans, it serves as an essential structural building block across diverse living organisms. In vertebrates, it is found most abundantly in connective tissues such as cartilage, tendons, and joint fluid; in arthropods, it is used to make chitin, a main component of their exoskeletons; in fungi, it is a major component of their rigid cell walls; and in bacteria, it is a vital part of the polymers that make their cell walls while also serving as a nutrient source [2]. Chitin is the structure that contains the highest proportion of glucosamine as it is made entirely of repeating chains of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc, a modified form of glucosamine).

Glucosamine in different organisms. Ai-generated image.

Commercial Glucosamine Production: Sources and Environmental Impacts

How are glucosamine sulfate and glucosamine HCI made?

Commercial glucosamine is usually produced by breaking down chitin sourced from crustacean processing byproducts or fungi, or through direct microbial fermentation using specialized strains of bacteria.

🦐 Crustacean Shell-derived Glucosamine

Commercial glucosamine is predominantly sourced from chitin extracted from discarded shells of crustaceans, especially shrimp, crab, and lobster generated by the large seafood industry. Shrimp and crab have been the dominant commercial chitin and chitosan feedstocks worldwide due to the popularity and availability of these seafood species, while lobster shells contribute to a smaller, niche research-focused sector [3].

Environmental Impacts of Crustacean-derived Glucosamine
+ Positive impacts

● Utilising Seafood Processing Byproducts: The global shellfish industry generates over 12-14 million tonnes of waste annually [4], creating a potentially abundant supply of raw material for chitin production. In this sense, chitin manufacturing offers a way to turn part of this waste into a useful resource while helping address the seafood waste problem.

− Caveats

● Disparity between demand and waste utilisation: Despite the abundance of raw material supply, in reality, only a tiny fraction of the discarded shells is currently utilised, including for chitin extraction. Much of the remainder ends up in landfills or is discharged into the sea, largely because of the costs and logistical challenges involved in collecting, storing, and processing it. As a result, much of the environmental burden remains unresolved, even as global demand for chitin and its derivatives remains strong and continues to grow [5].

● Environmental Costs of the Manufacturing Process: Chitin extraction and glucosamine production require strong acids and bases and generate substantial amounts of wastewater, adding environmental costs to the manufacturing process.

ℹ You might want to avoid krill-derived products: Antarctic krill processing byproducts from the pigment (astaxanthin) and krill oil industries can also be utilised for chitin extraction. These byproducts provide a high-yield, clean, consistent, and relatively low-mineral raw material for chitin production. However, Antarctic krill is a highly contentious source from an environmental perspective, with krill fisheries facing concerns related to overfishing, illegal and unregulated fishing, and climate change. Antarctic krill are a crucial component of Antarctic ecosystems and serve as a major food source for many marine predators, making them an important link in the Antarctic food web. Although regulatory management measures are in place, compliance and catch limits are not always guaranteed [6]. Since the 2000s, annual Antarctic krill catches have shown a continuing upward trend. As of 2025, Norway, China, South Korea, Chile, and Ukraine accounted for 100% of the reported Antarctic krill catch [7].

🧫 Fungi-derived glucosamine

Glucosamine can also be made from chitin extracted from the cell walls of filamentous fungi, which has the same chemical structure as chitin from shellfish. Fungal chitin offers a more environmentally friendly, vegan-friendly, and allergy-free source of glucosamine. The production process involves fungal fermentation, in which manufacturers feed a specific fungal strain, most commonly Aspergillus niger*, a nutrient-rich, plant-based sugar broth typically derived from corn or wheat. Once the fungi have grown into a dense, chitin-rich biomass, it is harvested and processed to extract and purify the chitin. The chitin can then undergo further processing, such as hydrolysis and crystallisation, to produce derivatives such as glucosamine or chitosan.

Environmental Impacts of Fungi-derived chitin & glucosamine
+ Positive impacts

● Less chemicals and resources used: Fungi-derived glucosamine does not require the same harsh chemical treatment of raw materials as shellfish-derived glucosamine, uses much less water, and generates less waste than traditional shellfish-derived production.

− Caveats

● Indirect drawbacks of raw materials: Fungi-derived glucosamine relies on fresh, plant-based raw materials such as corn or wheat, along with additional processing to produce the purified sugar nutrients needed to feed the fungi. Cultivating these crops comes with the environmental impacts of agriculture, including monoculture farming, arable land use, water consumption, and the use of fertilisers and pesticides.

🌽 Corn-derived glucosamine: direct microbial fermentation

There is a newer alternative method that bypasses the chitin intermediate by directly fermenting glucosamine from plant-derived glucose, particularly corn, using specialised engineered bacteria such as E. coli or yeast strains. These microorganisms convert glucose and nitrogen from the nutrient medium into glucosamine, which then undergoes downstream stabilisation to produce a mineral salt form such as glucosamine HCl or glucosamine sulfate. Other starchy plants such as wheat or soy may also be used instead of corn, providing an alternative for the smaller niche market of consumers with corn allergies. By eliminating the chitin extraction step, this method can use fewer resources and generate less waste than fungi-derived glucosamine production, while offering the same vegan-friendly, environmentally conscious, and allergy-free benefits.

Environmental Impacts of corn-derived glucosamine
+ Positive impacts

● Eco-friendly production: Corn-derived glucosamine offers several potential environmental advantages over traditional shellfish-derived glucosamine production, including lower water use, a lower carbon footprint, less waste generation, and reduced use of harsh chemicals.

− Caveats

● Indirect drawbacks of raw materials: Because corn or other starchy plants are used as the primary raw material, this method shares some of the environmental impacts of fungi-derived glucosamine, particularly those associated with crop agriculture. These include monoculture farming, arable land use, high water consumption, and the use of fertilisers and pesticides.

Alternative Chitin Sources with Limited Commercial Production

🦠 Microalgae

Chitin may also be extracted from microalgae, offering a potential green, low-impact source that requires less use of harsh chemicals, land, and water while generating less wastewater [8]. Despite this potential, algae-derived chitin is rarely used for commercial production due to low yields, expensive equipment, and the specialised technology required for its extraction. Nevertheless, algae are already used as a sustainable source of other high-value compounds, such as omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA), astaxanthin (a red-orange pigment with strong antioxidant properties), and other valuable pigments and proteins.

🦗 Insects

As environmental concerns rise, insects are being studied not only as an alternative protein source but also as a source of chitin. Their exoskeletons contain high levels of chitin, similar to those of crustaceans, while insect farming can require less land and water and may generate less waste. However, insect-derived chitin is currently used mainly for industrial and agricultural applications rather than human consumption, partly due to regulatory considerations and consumer acceptance compared with crustacean- or plant-derived sources.

Common Sources and Types of Glucosamine

🦐 Currently, crustacean-derived glucosamine dominates the market as a popular and affordable source, while corn-derived glucosamine occupies a more specialised market as a vegan, eco-friendly, and shellfish-free alternative.

💊 Glucosamine is commonly sold as glucosamine HCl because it contains a higher proportion of pure glucosamine by weight than glucosamine sulfate. This allows more glucosamine to be provided in the same capsule or tablet size. Glucosamine HCl can also be cheaper to produce because it does not require the additional processing needed to convert glucosamine into the stabilised sulfate form.

Verdicts: Which Glucosamine Source Is More Sustainable?

There is no single glucosamine source that is universally sustainable in absolute terms. Most, if not all, glucosamine sources come with existing or potential environmental impacts, with the main trade-offs depending on how their raw materials are sourced and processed.

♻️ Crustacean-derived glucosamine offers a cheaper product while making use of seafood processing waste generated by the massive fisheries and aquaculture industries. Its caveat is the processing waste generated during the treatment of raw materials and chitin extraction.

🌱 Fungi-derived and corn-derived glucosamine offer modern alternatives with less waste and no shellfish allergen. However, they do not make use of the abundant seafood waste generated by the fisheries and aquaculture industries, while also relying on plant materials whose cultivation can bring other types of environmental impacts associated with agricultural activities.

Other alternative sources are currently not viable for large-scale dedicated glucosamine production due to limitations in scale, economics, and regulatory considerations.

How to Make a Sustainable Choice When Buying Glucosamine
🌾➡🧑‍🌾➡🚛➡🏭➡💊

Environmentally conscious consumers should opt for products with traceable and transparent ingredients. There will always be trade-offs in manufacturing and large-scale production, but these impacts can be reduced by prioritising more sustainable raw materials. For instance, crustacean-derived glucosamine can be sourced from seafood produced through sustainable fisheries and aquaculture practices, while corn- or other plant-derived glucosamine can be produced using sustainably grown crops.

For more cascading impacts concerning glucosamine sources, check out this visualization from the WOO database.

ℹ Worth knowing

Global fisheries and aquaculture production was projected to reach 198 million tonnes in 2025 [9], with continued growth potential. This means the waste burden is unlikely to cease unless better solutions are developed or seafood consumption declines. With the world’s population projected to continue growing for at least another six decades [10], seafood consumption is unlikely to decline significantly, potentially increasing the waste burden and resource consumption in the coming years. This calls for less aggressive and more rigorous waste and byproduct processing, alongside better resource management strategies.

Applications of Chitin and its derivatives
🌾 🐛 🧪 💧 🩹 🧴

➔ Beyond glucosamine, chitin and its derivatives, such as chitosan, are gaining popularity for a wide range of applications, including agriculture (biostimulants, biopesticides), wastewater treatment (removing toxins and contaminants), medicine (bandages, wound dressings, tissue engineering), food and dietary products (food coatings, skincare, fat binders), and packaging (biodegradable packaging, biofilms, gelling agents). So far, demand for chitin remains consistently high, while barriers to processing raw materials prevent shell waste from being fully utilised, leaving a gap between supply and demand [11]. Solving these supply chain issues is a highly complex matter that requires global efforts. Finding alternative sources for chitin does not directly reduce seafood waste, while better extraction and processing technologies, together with local management at processing sites, might address the problem more directly.

*Aspergillus niger is a common dark brown to black, powdery filamentous fungus, also known as “black mold.” It is ubiquitous in the environment, particularly in air, soil, and decaying organic matter. The black, powdery mold commonly found on onion skins and necks is also most likely Aspergillus niger. In the environment, it can act as an opportunistic infectious agent and airborne allergen that may affect human health. Yet, it is also one of the most versatile microorganisms in biotechnology, particularly for the industrial production of citric acid.

⟶ READ NEXT: Glucosamine Effectiveness based on scientific literature

*MINI DISCLAIMER* This article draws on scientific and research literature and aims to present information about glucosamine sources, production methods, environmental impacts, and sustainability trade-offs as objectively as possible. It is intended solely for educational and informational purposes and should not be considered medical, environmental, or purchasing advice. Product sources and manufacturing practices can vary, and environmental impacts may differ between producers and production methods.
entry.summary: Where does glucosamine come from? Explore the crustacean, fungal, plant-based, microbial, and alternative sources used to produce glucosamine supplements, their production methods, environmental impacts, and the challenges of seafood waste and chitin supply

entry.title: Glucosamine Effectiveness: Clinical Evidence and Research. Does Glucosamine Actually Work for Osteoarthritis and Joint Health?

link.title: Glucosamine Effectiveness: Clinical Evidence and Research. Does Glucosamine Actually Work for Osteoarthritis and Joint Health?

entry.content:
Glucosamine and Joint Health: The Theory Behind Its Effectiveness

In the human body, glucosamine is an amino sugar found mostly in connective tissues, with the highest concentrations in articular cartilage, ligaments, tendons, and joint fluid. Hence, supplementing the body with glucosamine has been thought to benefit joint health and promote cartilage repair. However, its benefits have yet to be confirmed. Many studies have investigated the efficacy of glucosamine for joint health, osteoarthritis, and joint pain, but the results vary, leaving a definitive conclusion on its effectiveness somewhere in the mist.

This article summarises key findings from existing scientific literature and clinical studies examining glucosamine and its effects on human joint health, osteoarthritis, and joint pain, to provide a better understanding of the effectiveness of this widely used supplement.

Glucosamine Sulfate vs. Glucosamine HCl: What Is the Difference?

Glucosamine sulfate

A stable, crystalline form in which positively charged glucosamine molecules and negatively charged sulfate ions are held together, similar to magnets. This formulation receives widespread attention and favour in the supplement industry. Some medical experts believe it could serve a dual purpose in cartilage maintenance, as it provides both glucosamine and sulfate, substances involved in building cartilage. Glucosamine sulfate is available as a prescription-grade medicine in some European countries and as a dietary supplement in the United States, and often comes with a higher price than glucosamine HCl because its production requires additional processing to form and stabilise the sulfate salt.

Glucosamine Sulfate molecular structure.
National Center for Biotechnology Information. PubChem Compound Summary for CID 73415774, Glucosamine Sulfate. https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Glucosamine-Sulfate. Accessed Aug. 24, 2026.

Glucosamine hydrochloride (HCl)

A form of glucosamine produced by treating glucosamine free base (the uncharged form of pure glucosamine before it is converted into a salt), typically derived from chitin sourced from shellfish shells or fungi, or obtained through direct microbial fermentation, with hydrochloric acid to form a stable hydrochloride salt. Glucosamine HCl provides a higher concentration of glucosamine by weight than glucosamine sulfate and is often easier to formulate.

Glucosamine Hydrochloride molecular structure.
National Center for Biotechnology Information. PubChem Compound Summary for CID 91431, Glucosamine Hydrochloride. https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Glucosamine-Hydrochloride. Accessed Aug. 24, 2026.

ℹ The majority of glucosamine supplements on the market nowadays are combined with chondroitin sulfate, another naturally occurring sugar and component of joint cartilage, and sometimes MSM (methylsulfonylmethane), an organic sulfur-containing compound thought to also benefit joint health by acting as a sulfur donor.

Glucosamine Effectiveness: Does it really work? What Does the Evidence Show?

Glucosamine effectiveness remains uncertain, as clinical studies have produced mixed and sometimes conflicting results. In vitro and animal model studies of glucosamine suggest a positive role in cartilage building and function [1,2]. However, results from human clinical trials present a more complex story.

A significant number of clinical trials and studies have been conducted on the efficacy of glucosamine for joint pain and osteoarthritis (OA), with mixed results, leaving a definite conclusion elusive [3,4]. Although some studies have reported positive outcomes, the evidence supporting these findings has not been substantial enough to confirm glucosamine’s effectiveness, particularly given potential research biases such as conflicts of interest and industry sponsorship, as well as variations in study design and sample sizes. On the other hand, larger, independent studies have found little to no benefit from glucosamine compared with placebo [5–7].

A Cochrane review [8] assessing 25 studies involving 4,963 patients using glucosamine for OA found that:

  • Studies associated with the Rotta brand, including older and lower-quality studies, generally reported that glucosamine was effective in alleviating joint pain and improving joint function in OA patients.
  • High-quality, newer studies with rigorous controls, such as allocation concealment, that were not associated with the Rotta brand yielded mixed results for pain and function depending on the evaluation scale used. When measured using the Lequesne Index(※), the trials showed that glucosamine improved function and reduced pain compared with placebo. In contrast, studies measuring the results using the WOMAC Index(†) found no difference in pain or function compared with placebo.
  • In general, when all studies, including older, lower-quality, and Rotta-associated trials, were included in the evaluation, glucosamine showed positive effects on pain and function. However, results from non-Rotta preparations or studies with adequate allocation concealment showed no superiority over placebo for OA management.

A high-quality, large-scale, NIH-funded landmark study, the “Glucosamine/chondroitin Arthritis Intervention Trial” (GAIT), did not find glucosamine or chondroitin to be effective for OA pain relief, either when used alone or in combination [9]. A follow-up study from the same trial also suggested that neither glucosamine nor chondroitin, alone or in combination, prevented joint-space loss [10]. Nevertheless, exploratory analyses of these results found some potential pain-relieving effects from a combination of glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate in a subgroup of patients with moderate-to-severe knee pain, along with a potential slowing of joint-space loss in joints with mild or early damage.

These findings seem to align with the glucosamine research landscape of registered clinical trials from ClinicalTrials.gov(‡). The majority of glucosamine studies were conducted in the 2000s, and a much greater proportion were industry-/individual-/university-/ organisation-funded. Only a minority of trials have reported results and/or associated publications. Among the few trials with published papers, results vary depending on study design and quality, supporting the observation that larger-scale, higher-quality trials often found little to no difference in pain relief or cartilage function between groups using glucosamine and those taking placebo. Similarly, a handful of literature reviews that found glucosamine to be effective present potential reporting and selection biases [11,12], contributing to the uncertainty surrounding this substance.

Glucosamine Safety and Concerns: What Are the Risks and Recommendations?

Is glucosamine safe?

Low Concern

Glucosamine is relatively safe. Despite different outcomes in effectiveness, most studies have reported no significant safety concerns or noticeable adverse effects from using glucosamine for periods of up to 3 years.

Is Glucosamine Linked to Alzheimer’s Disease?

Preliminary Evidence

A recent study, published in June 2026 and funded by the NIH and other credible institutions [14], found that glucosamine supplementation may accelerate Alzheimer’s disease progression through a metabolic process called “hyperglycosylation,” in which complex sugar molecules excessively attach to proteins in brain cells and disrupt their normal function. As an amino sugar, additional glucosamine in an Alzheimer’s-affected brain could potentially worsen protein clumping and cellular stress, contributing to disease progression. Nevertheless, the findings have not established a definitive causal relationship, and the study suggests that glucosamine’s effects may be more relevant to brains with established Alzheimer’s disease rather than being a primary cause of the disease in otherwise healthy individuals.

Can Glucosamine Cause an Allergic Reaction If You Have a Shellfish Allergy?

Low Risk

Despite concerns over shellfish-derived glucosamine, scientific evidence suggests that the risk may depend on the purity of the product. The allergens responsible for shellfish allergy are proteins, mainly tropomyosin, found in the flesh and other tissues of shellfish, whereas glucosamine is derived from chitin in the hard outer shell. Hence, in theory, a highly purified glucosamine product without detectable shellfish proteins should not trigger a shellfish allergy. A clinical trial found that shrimp-allergic individuals tolerated 1,500 mg of glucosamine from specific brands without any incident of hypersensitivity [15]. Hence, it is reasonable to assume that whether a glucosamine product can trigger an allergic reaction depends largely on the purity and source of its ingredients.

How much glucosamine should be taken?

The standard dosage used in the majority of trials is 1,500 mg of glucosamine per day, consumed either once daily or divided into smaller doses. A study in horses found that glucosamine sulfate was better absorbed, penetrated the joints more effectively, and remained in the joint fluid longer than glucosamine HCl when administered orally [13]. However, there have been only a limited number of studies comparing the efficacy of the two forms.

What Are the Guidelines for Using Glucosamine?

Glucosamine is available as a prescription medicine in some European countries, but is generally marketed as a dietary supplement in the United States. Guidelines on its use differ across regions and regulatory bodies. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) and the American College of Rheumatology and Arthritis Foundation recommending against using glucosamine as a treatment for knee OA, while prescription-grade glucosamine sulfate might be prescribed for the same condition in some European countries [16,17].

Because glucosamine’s effectiveness remains equivocal, medical experts generally agree that its use can be tried for early-stage OA, but should be discontinued after 6 months if no improvement is observed [18,19]. Cost-effectiveness should also be taken into account for each individual use case [3].

ℹ Glucosamine and the Gut Microbiome: What Is the Potential Link?

Apart from its building-block role, glucosamine also serves as a food source for bacteria [20]. Some studies suggest that orally consumed glucosamine sulfate is poorly absorbed in the gut, with only around 10-12% being absorbed and more than 50% being utilised by gut bacteria. This raises the possibility that glucosamine supplements may also affect the gut microbiome, potentially contributing to their pain-relieving effects. Moreover, as the gut microbiome varies from individual to individual, differences in how glucosamine is processed by gut bacteria could potentially contribute to variations in its effects, perhaps helping explain the inconsistent results between clinical trials [21]. Nevertheless, this proposed mechanism remains poorly understood, and more studies are needed to determine how glucosamine is utilised by the gut microbiome and whether these changes contribute to its effects on joint health.

entry.title: What is Glucosamine: From Lobster Shells to One of the Most Popular Joint Health Supplements

link.title: What is Glucosamine: From Lobster Shells to One of the Most Popular Joint Health Supplements

entry.content:
Glucosamine is a naturally occurring amino sugar found across many living organisms, including plants, fungi, bacteria, and animals. In the human body, it is present in the highest concentrations in articular cartilage (the tissue covering joint surfaces), intervertebral discs (the cartilaginous cushions between the vertebrae of the spine), and synovial fluid (the lubricating fluid within movable joints). In these tissues, glucosamine serves as a precursor to glycosaminoglycans, long-chain complex sugars that combine with proteins to form proteoglycans - key components of the extracellular matrix that provide structure, resilience, hydration, and shock-absorbing properties to connective tissues such as cartilage and joints. Because of this role, glucosamine has become a popular ingredient in joint supplements, although clinical evidence for its effectiveness when consumed orally remains mixed.

Glucosamine as a building block for glycosaminoglycans & proteoglycans - Note: This image was generated using AI and may contain inaccuracies.

The Story of Glucosamine

1876

Glucosamine was first discovered by German orthopedic surgeon and scientist Georg Ledderhose, who isolated it by treating his leftover lobster shells with hydrochloric acid, yielding glucosamine hydrochloride (glucosamine HCl) - a solid, crystalline salt composed of glucosamine and chloride ions. He named the compound “glycosamine”.

Did you know? Georg Ledderhose is also the namesake of Ledderhose disease (plantar fibromatosis), a rare but benign condition he first documented in 1894. It is characterised by slow-growing, firm nodules that develop on the sole of the foot.

1898

A German chemist named Breuer created the first form of glucosamine sulfate by converting glucosamine hydrochloride into a sulfate salt. However, this remained primarily a laboratory experiment and did not advance into practical use at the time, as raw glucosamine sulfate was highly unstable and rapidly degraded when exposed to air and aqueous solutions.

1902

Hermann Leuchs, under the mentorship of Nobel laureate Emil Fischer, achieved the first total synthesis of glucosamine from arabinose - a 5-carbon sugar often found in plants, confirming its structure as an amino sugar. His work produced a pure, controlled sample of the glucosamine molecule and laid the groundwork for further studies in carbohydrate and structural chemistry, contributing to the understanding of amino sugars as fundamental building blocks of biological macromolecules and metabolic pathways.

1939

The British chemist Sir Walter Haworth, winner of a Nobel Prize in 1937, mapped the final 3D molecular structure and spatial arrangement (stereochemistry) of the glucosamine molecule that is still used today.

1930s - 1960s

This period marked a golden age of modern medicine and biochemistry, shaped by the rise of antibiotics, widespread vaccines, synthetic vitamins, antihistamines, and psychiatric medications, alongside major advances in biochemistry and molecular biology. These advances contributed to the understanding of metabolic pathways and helped elucidate the role of glucosamine in biological processes.

1960s - 1980s

As scientists recognised glucosamine’s role in the synthesis of biological macromolecules, they began investigating its potential therapeutic use in improving joint health. During this period, glucosamine sulfate was considered more effective than glucosamine HCl, as it contains glucosamine and sulfate - essential components in glycosaminoglycan synthesis and cartilage structure. However, due to its instability, glucosamine sulfate was not produced commercially or used clinically until the early 1980s, when Italian professor Luigi Rovati and his research group at Rottapharm developed a stabilised crystalline form - a mixed salt of glucosamine sulfate and sodium chloride (NaCl). This co-crystalline structure produced a stable, non-hygroscopic powder, in which the added salt helps stabilise the compound by reducing its exposure to moisture and oxygen. He patented the stabilised crystalline mixed salt form and its manufacturing process for prescription use in treating osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Worth noting: Professor Luigi Rovati was a physician and pharmacologist before leaving academia to establish a research laboratory in Monza, Italy, known as Rotta Research (later becoming Rottapharm). The company grew into a major pharmaceutical firm following the development of stabilised glucosamine sulfate (marketed as Dona). Parts of the business continue to operate today under the Rovati family as Rottapharm Biotech, with a presence in over 85 countries. Rottapharm is historically significant in the pharmaceutical industry, demonstrating that independent R&D can achieve major breakthroughs and scale globally.

1980s - present

During the 1980s, glucosamine was discovered to also have anti-inflammatory effects at the cellular level, where it helps slow the enzymes responsible for breaking down joint cartilage. This discovery further increased its therapeutic potential and popularity in the treatment of joint disorders, particularly osteoarthritis. Subsequently, extensive human clinical studies have been conducted since the late 1980s to evaluate its effectiveness.

Mid 1990s - 2000s

Glucosamine supplements reached peak popularity following the passage of the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA) of 1994 by the U.S. Congress, which classified glucosamine as an over-the-counter dietary supplement, as well as the influence of the 1997 best-selling book titled The Arthritis Cure by physician Jason Theodosakis.

Current Significance

As of present, glucosamine remains one of the most widely used joint health supplements globally, available in both sulfate and hydrochloride forms and most commonly formulated in combination with chondroitin sulfate. Its popularity continues amid growing demand for joint health products in aging populations. However, clinical evidence regarding its efficacy remains mixed, with conclusions varying across clinical trials, systematic reviews, and recommendations from different medical organisations.
